Family Health

Female pattern hair loss: recognising thinning and choosing care

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited byMohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

A widening part or gradual loss of fullness can be a sign of female pattern hair loss. The condition often develops slowly and becomes more common with age, but it can begin well before menopause. A clear diagnosis helps you choose care that fits your health, pregnancy plans, expectations and budget.

What female pattern hair loss means

Female pattern hair loss is a common cause of gradually thinning scalp hair. It is also called female pattern androgenetic alopecia. Follicles become smaller and produce finer, shorter hairs, making the scalp more visible even when hair is still growing. The change can be distressing, and asking for help is reasonable even when it is not a sign of serious illness.

The condition becomes more common with age and around or after menopause, but it can begin earlier, including in the twenties. It does not usually lead to complete baldness. A person’s age alone cannot establish the diagnosis or predict how much hair will be lost.

The usual pattern is a widening part or thinner crown

You may first notice a wider part, reduced fullness on the crown or a ponytail that feels less substantial. Some people also notice thinning at the temples. The front hairline is often relatively preserved, unlike the more typical receding pattern seen in men. Individual patterns still overlap.

Clinicians sometimes describe severity using the Ludwig scale: type I is mild thinning, type II has more visible thinning and a broader part, and type III has more marked loss with greater scalp visibility. These descriptions are a way to record appearance, not a timetable that everyone will follow.

Some daily shedding is normal; roughly 50 to 100 hairs is often quoted as a broad guide. Counting hairs in a brush cannot reliably diagnose pattern hair loss. Sudden handfuls of shedding, smooth round patches, broken hairs or an inflamed scalp can point to a different or additional condition.

Genes and hormones contribute in different ways

Inherited susceptibility may come from either side of the family. Hair follicles can respond differently to hormones even when blood hormone levels fall within the usual range. Female pattern hair loss therefore does not automatically mean that someone has excess testosterone or an endocrine disorder.

Irregular periods, new coarse facial or body hair, severe acne or other signs of androgen excess are reasons to discuss additional assessment. A clinician may consider conditions such as polycystic ovary syndrome when the whole history fits. Menopause-related changes can contribute to thinning, but assuming that every case is caused only by menopause can miss a treatable problem.

A diagnosis starts with the scalp and the history

A dermatologist will usually ask when the change began, whether it is sudden or gradual, and what has happened with illness, pregnancy, medicines, weight change, diet and hair styling. Examination may include the distribution of thinning, the condition of the scalp, a gentle hair-pull assessment and magnified inspection of the hairs and follicles.

Iron or thyroid tests and selected hormone tests may be useful when there is a reason to suspect a deficiency or another condition. They are not all necessary for everyone. Occasionally a small scalp biopsy helps distinguish pattern loss from inflammatory or scarring disease. Bring a medicine and supplement list and, if available, older photographs showing your usual part and hairline.

Set a realistic treatment goal

Treatment aims to slow further loss, preserve existing hair and sometimes improve density. It is easier to discuss realistic goals before buying a package promising complete restoration. Even a useful treatment may produce partial improvement rather than the hair volume someone had years earlier.

Hair grows slowly, so changes are assessed over months. Comparable photographs are often more helpful than checking the mirror every day. Many treatments need to continue to maintain their effect. Tell the clinician if you are pregnant, breastfeeding or planning pregnancy, because this can change which options are suitable.

Topical minoxidil is one established option

Minoxidil is applied to the scalp rather than taken as an ordinary hair vitamin. Products containing 2% or 5% are available, but authorised formulations, dosing schedules and directions vary by country and product. More concentrated or more frequent application is not automatically better. Follow the appropriate label and the clinician’s instructions.

Early increased shedding can occur when treatment begins. Irritation, dryness, itching or redness may make a product difficult to tolerate, and unwanted hair can grow on areas accidentally exposed to it. Apply only as directed and discuss troublesome effects rather than repeatedly increasing the amount.

It can take six to twelve months to judge the response. Benefits generally diminish after treatment is stopped. Minoxidil should not be started during pregnancy or when trying to conceive, and breastfeeding suitability needs professional advice; the American Academy of Dermatology advises avoiding it while nursing. Oral minoxidil is a different prescription decision, not an interchangeable way to use a topical product.

Spironolactone needs an individual prescription and monitoring

Spironolactone, sometimes sold as Aldactone, is a diuretic that also reduces the effects of androgens. Dermatologists may prescribe it off label for selected people with female pattern hair loss. Off label means the particular use is outside the medicine’s licence in that setting, not that it is automatically inappropriate.

Possible effects include increased urination, light-headedness from lower blood pressure, tiredness, breast tenderness and irregular periods. It can raise potassium, particularly in people with kidney problems or interacting medicines. The prescriber decides whether blood tests and blood-pressure checks are needed and when to repeat them.

Discuss pregnancy plans before starting. Spironolactone is avoided during pregnancy because of concern about effects on fetal sex development. Ask when to stop before trying to conceive and which contraception, if any, is appropriate for your situation. Do not copy a dose from another person’s hair-loss prescription.

Finasteride and dutasteride are specialist decisions

Finasteride, known by the brand Propecia in some settings, and dutasteride, often called Avodart, affect conversion of testosterone to dihydrotestosterone. Their use for female pattern hair loss is off label in many places and is considered only for selected patients. Evidence and suitability differ, so they are not routine substitutes for a diagnosis or first treatment discussion.

Their licences should not be conflated: in the United States, finasteride has an approved male-pattern hair-loss use, while the dutasteride label is for benign prostatic enlargement, not hair loss. Local approval and prescribing practice may differ.

These medicines must not be used during pregnancy because of the risk to development of a male fetus. A specialist should discuss pregnancy prevention where relevant, possible sexual or breast-related adverse effects, other reported symptoms, and the limited evidence for an individual patient. Do not share tablets or stop and restart them around pregnancy without medical guidance.

Supplements help only when the evidence fits the problem

If tests show iron deficiency, treating it may be important for health and hair growth. Taking extra iron without a reason can cause harm and does not guarantee thicker hair. A varied diet with appropriate sources of protein and iron, including beans, greens, fortified foods or other foods you eat, is more useful than assuming every hair problem needs a high-dose supplement.

Biotin and folic acid are frequently marketed for hair, but they are not established cures for pattern loss in people without a relevant deficiency. Biotin can also interfere with some laboratory tests, including certain heart-related tests. Tell clinicians and the laboratory about hair supplements before testing; do not stop prescribed pregnancy folic acid merely because it is not a hair-loss treatment.

A 2015 study followed 120 women for six months and reported improvement with a combination containing omega-3 and omega-6 fatty acids and antioxidants. This was a study of a particular combination, with limitations in the comparison and study design. It does not establish that any fish oil, individual ingredient or hair supplement will work, nor does it establish safety or benefit in pregnancy.

Laser devices and PRP have practical limits

Low-level light devices, such as some laser combs or caps, are offered for pattern hair loss. Device quality, study results, treatment schedules and regulatory status vary. Clearance for a particular device does not mean that every product using similar language is effective. Ask what evidence applies to the exact device and whether the expected improvement justifies the cost and time.

Platelet-rich plasma treatment involves drawing blood, concentrating a platelet-rich portion and injecting it into the scalp. It may be considered for selected patients, usually as a series with maintenance. It is not guaranteed to work and is not a one-time cure. Elective cosmetic PRP during pregnancy needs a separate safety discussion and is generally deferred.

Camouflage and transplant options serve different purposes

A wig, hairpiece, scalp powder, fibres or a change in hairstyle can improve the appearance of fullness without waiting for a medical treatment to work. These are legitimate choices, whether used alone or alongside treatment. Avoid attachments or tight styles that place persistent traction on fragile hair.

Hair transplantation moves follicles from a suitable donor area to thinning areas. Depending on the technique, follicles may be collected individually or from a strip of scalp. It redistributes existing follicles rather than creating new ones. Not everyone has an adequate donor area, and surgery does not stop ongoing thinning of untreated hair. Discuss scars, recovery, cost and the likely long-term treatment plan with an appropriately qualified surgeon.

Care for the hair you have while reviewing progress

Handle hair gently and limit practices that repeatedly damage it, such as high heat, harsh bleaching, frequent chemical processing or tight pulling styles. These changes can reduce breakage and traction but cannot reliably prevent inherited follicle changes. Protect exposed scalp from strong sun with a hat or suitable sunscreen.

Stopping smoking supports overall health; it should not be presented as a guaranteed cure for thinning. Likewise, a balanced diet does not eliminate genetic susceptibility. If a medicine may be contributing, discuss alternatives with its prescriber rather than stopping treatment yourself.

Arrange follow-up to compare photographs, tolerability and the result that matters to you. Seek earlier review for sudden or patchy loss, scalp pain, scaling, sores or signs of scarring. Emotional distress also deserves support. You do not have to continue an expensive or uncomfortable treatment simply because you have already invested time in it.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Dermatology guidance supports diagnosis-led care, with response to medicines assessed over months and maintenance often needed.

Pregnancy, breastfeeding, kidney health and interacting medicines can change treatment suitability.

How BeMama can help

Take a baseline photograph in ordinary lighting and bring a complete medicine and supplement list to your consultation.

When to seek help

Seek assessment for sudden or patchy loss or an inflamed scalp. Discuss pregnancy and breastfeeding before using hair-loss medicines, and tell clinicians about biotin before laboratory testing.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Pattern loss often widens the part while leaving the front hairline relatively preserved.
  • Normal hormone tests do not exclude female pattern hair loss.
  • Treatment can preserve or improve density but does not promise complete restoration.
  • Prescription medicines and supplements need individual safety checks.
  • Camouflage and choosing no medical treatment are valid options.

Frequently asked questions

Can it begin before menopause?

Yes. It becomes more common with age but can begin much earlier. Younger age should not prevent assessment of persistent thinning.

Does it mean I have too much testosterone?

Not necessarily. Many people have normal hormone levels. Irregular periods, severe acne or excess facial and body hair can make further hormone assessment appropriate.

Will I progress through every Ludwig stage?

No. The scale describes the visible degree of thinning. It does not predict that everyone will reach the most severe category.

How long should I try minoxidil before judging it?

It commonly takes six to twelve months to assess benefit, provided the product is appropriate and tolerated. Follow the plan and report adverse effects rather than increasing the dose yourself.

Can I use hair-loss medicines while pregnant?

Several common treatments are avoided in pregnancy, including minoxidil, spironolactone, finasteride and dutasteride. Discuss pregnancy plans before starting or continuing treatment.

Why might spironolactone require blood tests?

It can affect potassium and may be unsuitable with kidney problems or interacting medicines. The clinician chooses monitoring based on your individual risks.

Is dutasteride approved for hair loss everywhere?

No. Approval varies, and its United States label is for benign prostatic enlargement. Hair-loss prescribing may be off label and needs a specialist discussion.

Should I take biotin or iron just in case?

Not automatically. A deficiency should be assessed when suspected. Extra iron can be harmful, and biotin can distort some blood-test results without being an established cure for pattern hair loss.

Does the omega supplement study prove fish oil will regrow my hair?

No. It tested a particular multi-ingredient combination in a limited study. The result cannot be transferred to every supplement or to pregnancy.

Will a transplant stop future hair loss?

No. It moves existing follicles to another area and does not stop thinning of the remaining hair. Suitability and long-term care need discussion before surgery.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
